title: The Young Runner's First Marathon
summary: A girl who has been building up her running distance for months trains with her coach for her school district's biggest fun run, and learns how pacing and mental endurance help her finish strong.
poll: Going slow and steady is a better way to win than running as fast as you can.

versions.title: Noor Learns to Run
versions.text:
Noor loved to run. She ran every day. Coach Reem helped her train.

Long ago, Noor could run just one kilometer. Then she got tired fast. Coach Reem made a plan. Each week, Noor ran a bit more.

The school had a big race. It was the Fun Run. It was five kilometers long. It was the longest race at her school.

Coach Reem said, “Do not run fast at the start. Keep one pace. Save your strength.”

On race day, some kids ran fast at the start. Noor did not. She kept one slow pace.

Her legs got tired. Her mind got tired, too. She said, “I can do this.” She thought of her practice.

Noor ran all five kilometers. She did not stop. She crossed the finish line!

Coach Reem smiled. “You did it,” she said. “One day, you can run a real marathon.”

Noor felt proud. She learned to go slow and steady. She did not give up.

Noor loved running more than any other sport at her school. She trained every day. Her coach, Coach Reem, was kind. But she was also always firm about training hard.

Months earlier, Noor could barely run one kilometer. Then she grew too tired to continue. Coach Reem designed a careful training plan for her. Each week, Noor ran a little farther than she had the week before. Slowly, she was building her strength.

One spring, the school district announced its biggest race of the year. It was called the Fun Run. It stretched a full five kilometers. That made it the longest race the district held all year. Many students felt nervous about running so far.

Before the race, Coach Reem gave Noor some important advice. “Do not sprint at the start,” she explained. “Keep one steady pace for the whole race. Save your strength for the final part.”

On race day, several students sprinted ahead the moment the race began. Noor refused to copy them. Instead, she kept a slow, steady pace. She held this pace from her very first step.

Partway through, her legs grew heavy and tired. Her mind grew tired, too. It was urging her to stop. She kept repeating to herself, “I can do this.” She thought carefully about every week of hard practice.

Noor ran the entire five kilometers without stopping. She passed several students who had sprinted early. They were now walking. Finally, she crossed the finish line, tired but smiling with pride.

Coach Reem smiled a huge, proud smile. “You did it,” she said warmly. “Someday, when you are older and ready, you could train for a real marathon.”

Noor felt extremely proud of herself that day. She had learned that going slow and steady beats rushing carelessly. She had also learned to never give up, even when something feels hard.

versions.title: Noor and the Fun Run
versions.text:
Noor loved running more than any other sport at her school. She trained every day without fail. Her coach, Coach Reem, was kind but firm. She always said that training wisely mattered more than training fast.

Months earlier, Noor could barely finish one kilometer. Then she grew too tired to continue. Coach Reem designed a training plan that built up her distance gradually. Slowly, this gave Noor more stamina for longer runs.

One spring, the school district announced its biggest race of the year. It was called the Fun Run. It covered a full five kilometers. That made it the longest race the district held all year. Noor's friend Lina felt nervous about running so far for the first time.

Before the race, Coach Reem shared her strategy for pacing. “Do not sprint at the start just because you feel excited,” she explained. “Keep one steady pace. Save your strength for the final stretch, where you will need it most.”

On race day, several classmates sprinted ahead the instant the race began. One of them was a boy named Yusuf. Noor refused to copy them. She kept a slow, steady pace from her very first step.

Partway through, around the third kilometer, her legs grew heavy. Her mind grew tired as well. It was quietly urging her to stop. She repeated a short phrase to encourage herself: “I can do this.” She thought about every week of patient practice.

Noor ran the entire five kilometers without stopping. She passed Yusuf and others who had sprinted early. They were now walking near the end. Finally, she crossed the finish line, exhausted but beaming with pride.

Coach Reem hugged her. “You did it,” she said warmly. “A real marathon is about forty-two kilometers, far longer than today's race. But someday, when you are older, you could train for one.”

Noor felt extremely proud that afternoon. She had learned that slow and steady usually beats rushing carelessly. She had also learned that never giving up matters just as much as speed.

versions.title: Noor and the Fun Run
versions.text:
Noor loved running more than any other sport at her school, and she trained every single day without fail, regardless of the weather or how tired she felt. Her coach, Coach Reem, was kind but consistently firm, frequently reminding her students that sprinting at full speed from the very start was rarely the most effective strategy for a genuinely long race.

Months earlier, Noor could barely finish one kilometer before growing too exhausted to continue any farther. Coach Reem designed a careful, patient training plan that built up Noor's distance gradually, kilometer by kilometer, without ever rushing the process, slowly developing both the strength and the mental endurance she would need on race day itself.

One spring, the school district announced its biggest race of the year, known as the Fun Run. It covered a full five kilometers, by far the longest race the district held all year, considerably longer than anything the younger students usually attempted in gym class. Noor's close friend Lina felt genuinely anxious about the unfamiliar distance.

Before the race, Coach Reem explained her pacing strategy, a skill that separates experienced runners from beginners. “Do not sprint at the start simply because you feel excited or nervous,” she said. “Keep one steady pace for the entire race, and save your strength for the final stretch, where you will truly need it most.”

On race day, several classmates, including a boy named Yusuf, sprinted ahead the instant the signal sounded, fueled by excitement rather than strategy. Noor refused to copy their pace, choosing instead a slow, deliberate rhythm from her very first step.

Partway through, around the third kilometer, the exertion made her legs ache, and her mind grew weary too, quietly urging her to give up. She repeated a phrase to motivate herself: “I can do this.” It took real fortitude to sustain her effort and think only of her months of patient practice. This stubborn determination is what coaches call mental endurance.

Noor ran the entire five kilometers without stopping, steadily overtaking Yusuf and others who had sprinted early and were now walking near the final kilometer, their energy completely depleted. Finally, she crossed the finish line, exhausted but beaming with pride.

Coach Reem hugged her tightly. “You did it,” she said warmly. “A real marathon measures about forty-two kilometers, far longer than today's race, but someday, when your body has had years to develop, you could train carefully for one, exactly as you trained for this.”

Noor felt prouder that afternoon than after any previous race. She had learned that going slow and steady usually outperforms rushing carelessly, and that mental endurance, the will to keep going even when your mind wants to quit, matters every bit as much as natural speed.

keyWords.definition: a person who trains and helps athletes get better at a sport
keyWords.example: Our coach taught us how to pass the ball better.

keyWords.definition: the speed you move at, especially while running
keyWords.example: He kept a slow pace so he would not get tired too soon.

keyWords.definition: to come to the end of something, like a race
keyWords.example: She wanted to finish the puzzle before dinner.

keyWords.definition: a very long running race, about forty-two kilometers
keyWords.example: My uncle trained for a whole year before he ran his first marathon.

keyWords.definition: doing something again and again to get better at it
keyWords.example: With enough practice, Ali learned to swim across the pool.

questions.stem: How did Noor train before the race?
options: She ran a little more each week
She only ran on the day of the race
She watched other runners on television
She stopped running for a month
questions.why: In the story, Coach Reem made a plan, and each week Noor ran a bit more than the week before.

wrong.B: Noor trained for months, not just one day.
wrong.C: The story does not mention watching television.
wrong.D: Noor never stopped running during her training.

questions.stem: What did Coach Reem tell Noor to do at the start of the race?
options: Run as fast as she can right away
Keep a slow, steady pace
Wait until everyone else finishes
Stop after one kilometer
questions.why: Coach Reem told Noor not to run fast at the start and to keep one steady pace.

wrong.A: Coach Reem told her the opposite: not to run fast at the start.
wrong.C: Noor ran the whole race herself; she did not wait.
wrong.D: The story does not say to stop after one kilometer.

questions.stem: In the story, pace means —

the speed a runner moves at
the finish line of a race
a kind of race medal
questions.why: The story talks about keeping a steady pace, meaning the speed Noor runs at.

wrong.A: The story does not talk about shoe color.
wrong.C: The finish line is a different thing from pace.
wrong.D: The story does not mention medals.

questions.stem: What happened to some kids who sprinted at the start of the race?
options: They won the race easily at the end
They got tired and had to walk later
They stopped to help Noor on the track
They ran the race twice in one day

wrong.A: The story does not say they won.
wrong.C: They did not stop to help Noor.
wrong.D: No one ran the race twice.

questions.stem: Why did Noor say "I can do this" to herself during the race?
options: To remember her shopping list
To help her keep going when she felt tired
To tell Coach Reem she wanted to stop
To count how many kids were ahead of her
questions.why: Noor's legs and mind were tired, so she repeated these words to push through and keep running.

wrong.A: The story is not about shopping.
wrong.C: She was not telling Coach Reem to stop; she kept running.
wrong.D: The story does not say she was counting runners.

questions.stem: What can you tell about Noor from the fact that she trained every day for months?
options: She did not care about the race
She was determined and hardworking
She wanted to quit the team
She was already the fastest runner

wrong.C: She never wanted to quit; she kept training.
wrong.D: The story says she could only run one kilometer at first, not that she was already fastest.

questions.stem: Why does Coach Reem say Noor could run a real marathon one day?

Because Noor is older than her friends and taller than the coach
Because Noor showed she can build up distance and keep going
Because the school has no more races, so she must run in a big one

wrong.B: The story does not compare her age to her friends.
wrong.D: The story does not say the school stops having races.

LOW.prompt: Would you rather run fast at the start of a race or keep a slow, steady pace? Explain your answer using at least two facts from the story.
checklist: I clearly said which way I would choose.
I used at least two facts from the story.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: I would rather keep a slow, steady pace like Noor did. In the story, the kids who sprinted at the start got tired and had to walk later in the race. Noor kept one steady pace the whole time, and she was able to run all five kilometers without stopping. I think going slow and steady is smarter than running too fast at the beginning.

keyWords.definition: the energy and strength to keep doing something hard for a long time
keyWords.example: Climbing the mountain trail took real stamina.

keyWords.definition: a careful plan for reaching a goal
keyWords.example: The team used a new strategy to win the game.

keyWords.definition: extremely tired, with very little energy left

keyWords.definition: to give someone support or confidence to keep trying
keyWords.example: Her older sister tried to encourage her before the spelling test.

keyWords.definition: happening slowly, a little bit at a time
keyWords.example: The puppy gradually learned to sit when asked.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the story?
options: Noor trains patiently for months and uses a steady pace and determination to finish her school district's biggest race.
Noor decides running is too hard, so she quits the team and never goes to any practice again, even with Coach Reem.
Lina wins the Fun Run while Noor finishes last, and Noor feels sad about her slow pace.
Coach Reem cancels the Fun Run because it is too long, and the students go home early.
questions.why: The story follows Noor's months of training, her pacing strategy, and her determination to finish the district's longest race.

wrong.B: Noor never quits; she keeps training and finishes the race.
wrong.C: The story does not describe Lina winning or Noor finishing last.
wrong.D: The race is held as planned; it is not canceled.

questions.stem: How did Noor's training change over the weeks before the race?
options: She ran the same one kilometer every single week
She gradually ran a little farther each week
She trained only in the final week before the race
She switched from running to swimming
questions.why: Coach Reem's plan had Noor run a little farther than the week before, building up her distance gradually over time.

wrong.A: Noor's distance increased each week instead of staying the same.
wrong.C: Her training happened over many weeks, not just the final one.
wrong.D: The story stays focused on running, not swimming.

questions.stem: How long is the Fun Run, and what does that make it for the district?
options: Two kilometers, the shortest race of the year for the district
Five kilometers, the longest race the district holds all year
Ten kilometers, a race only adults can enter in the district
One kilometer, a race just for younger students in the district
questions.why: In the story, the Fun Run covers five kilometers and is the longest race the district holds all year.

wrong.A: The Fun Run is the longest race, not the shortest.
wrong.C: The race is five kilometers, not ten, and students run it.
wrong.D: The race is for students like Noor, and it is five kilometers, not one.

questions.stem: What happened because Yusuf and other students sprinted at the start of the race?
options: They finished the race first by a wide margin
They were disqualified from the race
They ran out of energy and had to walk later
They decided to help Noor pace herself
questions.why: Because they sprinted early without a pacing strategy, Yusuf and the others grew exhausted and were walking by the final kilometer, while Noor passed them.

wrong.A: Noor passed them later in the race, so they did not finish first.
wrong.B: The story never mentions anyone being disqualified.
wrong.D: They were walking from exhaustion, not helping Noor.

questions.stem: In the story, the word gradually means —
options: all at once, very suddenly
a little at a time, slowly
only during the summer
with no plan at all
questions.why: Noor's distance built up gradually, meaning her training added a little more each week rather than all at once.

wrong.A: Gradually is the opposite of all at once.
wrong.C: The word has nothing to do with a season.
wrong.D: Coach Reem's careful training plan is the opposite of having no plan.

questions.stem: Why did Noor keep repeating "I can do this" during the third kilometer?
options: To encourage herself to keep going even though she felt tired
To remind herself of the route back to school and the road
To practice speaking loudly for a school play in the hall
To tell Lina to slow down because she was so tired
questions.why: Noor's legs and mind were growing tired, so repeating this phrase helped encourage herself to push through the hard part of the race.

wrong.B: The phrase is about determination, not directions.
wrong.C: The story has nothing to do with a school play.
wrong.D: The story does not say Noor spoke to Lina during this moment.

questions.stem: How does the author organize the events of the story?
options: By comparing two different schools in every paragraph, from their gyms to their teachers and their sports days
By following Noor's training, the race itself, and then her success afterward, in time order
By explaining rules for several different sports, one by one, from football to tennis
By listing facts about marathons around the world, from the oldest to the newest race
questions.why: The story moves in time order: Noor's months of training, Coach Reem's advice, the race day events, and the celebration at the finish line.

wrong.A: The story focuses on one school's team, not a comparison between schools.
wrong.C: The story focuses on running, not several sports.
wrong.D: The story does not list facts about marathons worldwide.

questions.stem: Why does Coach Reem explain that a real marathon is about forty-two kilometers?
options: To scare Noor away from running longer races for good, since they are too hard for her
To show that the Fun Run was a fair, age-appropriate step toward a much bigger future goal
To tell Noor she must run a marathon next week, in the big city race
To explain why the Fun Run was canceled that day, due to the heat
questions.why: Coach Reem's comment places the five-kilometer Fun Run in context, showing it is a sensible milestone that could one day lead to a full marathon when Noor is older.

wrong.A: Coach Reem is encouraging Noor, not scaring her.
wrong.C: Coach Reem says "someday," not next week.
wrong.D: The race happened as planned; it was not canceled.

MID.prompt: Explain how Noor's training and her pacing strategy helped her succeed in the Fun Run. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I explained how Noor's training helped her.
I explained how her pacing strategy helped her.
I used at least two details from the story.
MID.modelAnswer: Noor's training helped her succeed because Coach Reem built up her distance gradually, so by race day her body was ready to run five kilometers. Her pacing strategy also helped: instead of sprinting at the start like Yusuf and other students, she kept one steady pace the whole race. Because of this, she still had energy left near the end, while the students who sprinted early had to slow down to a walk. Her training and her strategy worked together to help her finish strong.

keyWords.definition: the ability to keep doing something difficult for a long time without giving up
keyWords.example: Long hikes in the desert require real endurance.

keyWords.definition: the physical or mental effort used to do something hard
keyWords.example: After the exertion of the climb, the hikers rested in the shade.

keyWords.definition: the inner strength to face pain or difficulty calmly and without giving up
keyWords.example: The sailors showed great fortitude during the long storm.

keyWords.definition: to give someone a reason or the energy to keep trying

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of the story?
options: Natural talent alone decides who finishes a long race.
Patient training and steady pacing let Noor outlast faster, less careful runners.
Running fast at the very start of a race is always the wisest possible plan.
A coach becomes unnecessary once a runner trains for a few weeks.
questions.why: The story shows that gradual training, pacing, and mental endurance, not raw talent or early speed, let Noor outlast runners like Yusuf who started faster.

wrong.A: Noor's success comes from training and strategy, not natural talent.
wrong.C: The story shows the opposite: runners who sprinted early ended up walking.
wrong.D: Coach Reem's guidance stays essential throughout Noor's training.

questions.stem: Why does the story mention that Noor could run only one kilometer months before the race?
options: It shows that Noor was never a capable athlete.
It gives a reason she quit the running team.
It sets a clear starting point that shows how much her training changed.
It compares her unfavorably with Yusuf and his early burst of speed.
questions.why: Starting from a limited ability makes the gradual, weekly progress of her training plan, and her eventual finish, far more meaningful to the reader.

wrong.A: The story instead shows her becoming more capable over time.
wrong.B: Noor never quits; she keeps training and competing.
wrong.D: The comparison with Yusuf comes later, during the race itself.

questions.stem: According to Coach Reem's advice, what is the main risk of sprinting at the start of a long race?
options: A runner may be disqualified by race officials.
A runner may confuse the other competitors running nearby on the course.
A runner may finish too quickly to be timed accurately.
A runner may run out of strength before the hardest final stretch.
questions.why: Coach Reem explains that sprinting early wastes strength a runner will need later, which is exactly what happens to Yusuf and the other students.

wrong.A: Disqualification is never mentioned in the story.
wrong.B: Confusing other runners is not the risk Coach Reem describes.
wrong.C: The story is not concerned with finishing too quickly to be timed.

questions.stem: In the story, the term mental endurance most precisely refers to —
options: a runner's natural speed over short distances
the determination to keep going even when the mind wants to stop
a coach's ability to design a training schedule
The official distance of a marathon race, measured in kilometers.
questions.why: The story defines mental endurance through Noor's experience: repeating "I can do this" to keep going even as her tired mind urges her to quit.

wrong.A: Mental endurance is about willpower, not raw speed.
wrong.C: Designing a schedule is Coach Reem's role, not the meaning of this term.
wrong.D: The marathon's distance is a separate fact in the story.

questions.stem: Based on the story, why did Noor's friend Lina, like other students, feel anxious before the race?
options: Five kilometers was far beyond any distance they had attempted before.
They disliked their coach's training methods.
They believed the race would be canceled because of bad weather.
They had never met students from other schools.
questions.why: In the story, five kilometers was considerably longer than any distance the students usually ran in gym class, which explains their anxiety.

wrong.B: The story gives no sign that students disliked Coach Reem's methods.
wrong.C: Nothing suggests the students expected the race to be canceled.
wrong.D: Meeting other schools is not shown as a source of their anxiety.

questions.stem: Place these events from the story in the correct order.
options: The race begins; Noor struggles to run one kilometer; Coach Reem designs a plan.
Coach Reem explains the marathon distance; Noor struggles with one kilometer; the race begins.
Noor struggles to run one kilometer; Coach Reem designs a plan; Noor crosses the finish line.
Noor crosses the finish line; Coach Reem designs a plan; Noor struggles with one kilometer.
questions.why: Noor's early struggle with one kilometer comes first, followed by Coach Reem's gradual training plan, and finally Noor's finish at the race.

wrong.A: The race begins only after months of training, not before Noor's early struggles.
wrong.B: Coach Reem explains the marathon distance after the race, not before.
wrong.D: This places the finish before the training that made it possible.

questions.stem: What can readers infer about Yusuf from the fact that he was walking by the final kilometer?
options: He had sustained his early pace successfully all the way to the end.
He had decided to stop and cheer for Noor instead.
He had injured himself before the race even began.
He had skipped a pacing strategy and used up his energy too soon.
questions.why: Because Yusuf sprinted without pacing himself, he could not sustain his effort and ran out of energy before the end, unlike Noor's steady approach.

wrong.A: Walking by the end shows he could not sustain his early pace.
wrong.B: Nothing in the story suggests he stopped to cheer for Noor.
wrong.C: No injury before the race is mentioned.

questions.stem: Why does the story end by saying Noor's lesson applied to challenges "both on and off the running track"?
options: To hint that Noor plans to switch to a different sport entirely next year
To suggest that pacing and determination help with more than just running
To indicate that the story's events were only a dream at night
To argue that running matters less than other activities in school
questions.why: This closing line broadens the story's theme, suggesting that the patience and mental endurance Noor developed can help her in other parts of life, not just races.

wrong.A: There is no suggestion that Noor is switching sports.
wrong.C: Nothing in the story frames these events as a dream.
wrong.D: The story never says running matters less than other activities.

HIGH.prompt: The poll states that going slow and steady is a better way to win than running as fast as you can. Do you agree or disagree? Support your position with evidence from the story about Noor's training, her pacing strategy, and what happened to the runners who sprinted early.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that going slow and steady is often a better strategy than sprinting as fast as possible. In the story, Noor trained gradually for months, slowly building her stamina until she could run the full five kilometers without stopping. During the race itself, she maintained one steady pace instead of sprinting like Yusuf and the other students, and this pacing strategy allowed her to sustain her effort to the very end. Meanwhile, the runners who sprinted early exhausted themselves and were reduced to walking before the finish line. Someone might argue that sprinting works for very short races, where there is no time to run out of energy, but for a demanding five-kilometer distance like the Fun Run, Noor's patient, steady approach clearly produced the better result.

options: Her friend Lina will join her later

She chose a steady rhythm based on a plan
She waited to hear the signal
